subtopics.name: Lattice Energy & Enthalpy Change of Atomisation
Electron Affinity & Trends of Group 16 & 17 Elements

parts.problem_md: Define the term lattice energy.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of lattice energy:
> 
> - The energy change (or enthalpy change) when one mole of an ionic compound is formed **[1 mark]**
> - From its constituent gaseous ions, under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Learn all thermodynamic definitions for CIE IAL Chemistry. Lattice energy is always exothermic (negative), as forming ionic bonds from gaseous ions releases energy.

parts.problem_md: Construct an equation, including state symbols, to represent the first electron affinity of chlorine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equation for the first electron affinity of chlorine is:
> 
> - Cl (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be included for the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> ½Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) is not an acceptable answer because this represents both the enthalpy of atomisation and the electron affinity, not just the electron affinity.

parts.problem_md:
Some energy changes are shown in Table 1.1.

**Table 1.1**

| **Energy change** | **Value / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Standard enthalpy change of formation of MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –641 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of magnesium | +148 |
| First ionisation energy of magnesium | +738 |
| Second ionisation energy of magnesium | +1450 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine | +121 |
| Lattice energy, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>, of magnesium chloride, MgCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –2526 |

Calculate the first electron affinity of chlorine. Use relevant data from Table 1.1 in your working.

Show your working.

It may be helpful to draw a labelled energy cycle.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the first electron affinity of chlorine:

![Born-Haber cycle for MgCl2 showing enthalpy changes with values in kJ mol^-1^](assets/001-born-haber-cycle-for-mgcl2-showing-enthalpy-chan.png)

- Use the Born-Haber relationship:

Δ*H*<sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(Mg) + IE<sub>1</sub>(Mg) + IE<sub>2</sub>(Mg) + 2Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(Cl) + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) + Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub>(MgCl<sub>2</sub>)

–641 = 148 + 738 + 1450 + 2(121) + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) + (–2526) **[1 mark]**

- Simplify:

–641 = 52 + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) **[1 mark]**

2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) = –693 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

- Calculate the result:

EA<sub>Cl</sub> = **–346.5 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for correct Born-Haber equation with correct substitution
> **OR**
> 1 mark for a correctly drawn and labelled Born-Haber cycle
> 
> 1 mark for correct simplification: –641 = 52 + 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>)
> **OR**
> 2(EA<sub>Cl</sub>) = –693 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for EA<sub>Cl</sub> = –346.5 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating using a Born-Haber cycle, always check:
> 
> - Correct values from the data table
> - Lattice energy is negative (energy released on forming the solid)
> - Correct multipliers for the formula (MgCl<sub>2</sub> contains 2 Cl, so use 2 x EA<sub>Cl</sub> and 2 x Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(Cl))
> 
> A very common error is forgetting the stoichiometry of the chlorine. Since the formula is MgCl<sub>2</sub>, two chloride ions are formed. Therefore both the enthalpy of atomisation of chlorine and the electron affinity must be multiplied by 2.

parts.problem_md: Explain, in terms of ionic radius, charge density and polarisation, why the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group because:
> 
> - The ionic radius of the Group 2 cation (M<sup>2+</sup>) increases down the group **[1 mark]**
> - The charge density of M<sup>2+</sup> decreases as a result **[1 mark]**
> - There is less polarisation / less distortion of the CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup> ion by the cation **[1 mark]**
> - The C–O bonds are weakened less, so a higher temperature is needed to decompose the carbonate **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Students often lose marks on questions like this by mixing up cause and effect.
> 
> Make sure you clearly connect the chain:
> 
> - larger cation
> - → lower charge density
> - → less polarisation of CO<sub>3</sub><sup>2-</sup>
> - → C–O bonds less weakened
> - → harder to decompose
> - → greater thermal stability.
> 
> When explaining polarisation, focus on the carbonate anion and use the word "polarisation" or "distortion" explicitly. Restating that thermal stability increases does not explain the underlying reason.

parts.problem_md: Predict and explain the sign of the standard entropy change, Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>, for the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s).
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The sign of Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> for the decomposition of MgCO<sub>3</sub> (s) is:
> 
> - Positive
> **OR**
> Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup> > 0 **[1 mark]**
> - A gas (CO<sub>2</sub>) is produced from solid reactants, increasing the number of gaseous particles and therefore increasing disorder/entropy **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When explaining entropy changes, focus on what happens to the particles, not just the states of matter involved.
> 
> Many students lose marks by writing vague statements such as "a solid turns into a gas" without explaining that a gas is produced from solids, which increases disorder.
> 
> In entropy questions, always check whether the number of gaseous particles increases, as this is usually the dominant factor affecting Δ*S*<sup>θ</sup>.

parts.problem_md: Define the term lattice energy.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of lattice energy:
> 
> - Formation of 1 mole of an ionic lattice from its constituent gaseous ions **[1 mark]**
> - Under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> There are many thermodynamic definitions you need to know for CIE IAL Chemistry. They are typically worth 2 or 3 marks and are worth memorising.

parts.problem_md:
The Born-Haber cycle in Fig. 1.1 can be used to determine the lattice energy of calcium oxide.

Steps **A**–**G** include the values for enthalpy changes.

Complete the Born-Haber cycle by adding the species present on the two dotted lines.

Include state symbols.

![Born-Haber cycle for the formation of calcium oxide showing steps A to G](assets/002-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-calcium-ox.png)

**Fig. 1.1**
parts.solution_md:
The missing species are:

- (Step **E**) Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) + O (g) + 2e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
- (Step **G**) Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) + O<sup>2-</sup>(g) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Step E in the Born-Haber cycle begins with Ca<sup>+</sup>(g) + O (g) + 2e<sup>-</sup>. The calcium ion needs to lose another electron to form a 2+ ion (second ionisation energy), so Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) + O (g) + 2e<sup>-</sup> is the missing species.
> 
> Step G represents the second electron affinity of oxygen. This is the enthalpy change when one mole of O<sup>-</sup>(g) ions forms one mole of O<sup>2-</sup>(g) ions. As shown in the Born-Haber cycle, Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) + O<sup>-</sup>(g) + e<sup>-</sup> becomes Ca<sup>2+</sup>(g) + O<sup>2-</sup>(g).
> 
> Examiners often ask about the second electron affinity of oxygen, so make sure you know it well.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

The Born-Haber cycle in Fig. 1.1 can be used to determine the lattice energy of calcium oxide.

Steps **A**–**G** include the values for enthalpy changes.

Identify the enthalpy changes represented by steps **B**, **D** and **F** in the Born-Haber cycle.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The enthalpy changes represented by each step are:
> 
> - (**B**) enthalpy change of atomisation (of calcium) **[1 mark]**
> - (**D**) first ionisation energy (of calcium) **[1 mark]**
> - (**F**) first electron affinity (of oxygen) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The enthalpy change of atomisation is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from an element in its standard state, for example Ca (s) → Ca (g).
> 
> The first ionisation energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is removed from one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous ions with a single positive charge, for example Ca (g) → Ca<sup>+</sup>(g).
> 
> The first electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one mole of electrons to form one mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge, for example O (g) → O<sup>-</sup>(g).

parts.problem_md:
Step **C** represents the enthalpy change of atomisation of oxygen.

Explain why the enthalpy change of atomisation is always endothermic.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The enthalpy change of atomisation is always endothermic because:
> 
> - Energy must be absorbed to break the bonds in the element **[1 mark]**
> - No bond forming occurs in this process, so no energy is released **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The enthalpy change of atomisation is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms is formed from an element in its standard state, for example O<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2O (g).
> 
> This process is always endothermic because bond breaking requires energy input, and no bond forming occurs to release energy.
> 
> Remember that endothermic reactions always have positive enthalpy changes and exothermic reactions have negative enthalpy changes.

parts.problem_md:
Magnesium oxide is often used in optical applications due to its light-reflecting properties in crystal form.

Write an equation to represent the lattice energy of MgO.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> An equation to represent the lattice energy of MgO is:
> 
> - Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + O<sup>2-</sup> (g) → MgO (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols and ionic charges are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.
> 
> For magnesium oxide, the equation is Mg<sup>2+</sup> (g) + O<sup>2-</sup> (g) → MgO (s). Both state symbols and the correct ionic charges (2+ and 2–) must be shown.

parts.problem_md:
Use the data in Table 2.1 to calculate a value for the second ionisation energy of magnesium, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>. Show your working.

**Table 2.1**

| **Enthalpy change** | **Enthalpy change / kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| Lattice energy of MgO (s) | – 3791 |
| Enthalpy change of atomisation of Mg | + 148 |
| Enthalpy of atomisation of oxygen | + 248 |
| Electron affinity of the oxygen atom | – 141 |
| Electron affinity of the oxygen anion, O<sup>-</sup> | + 798 |
| First ionisation energy of Mg | + 736 |
| Enthalpy of formation of MgO | – 552 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the second ionisation energy of magnesium:

- Write the Born-Haber equation relating all enthalpy changes:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Mg) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie1</sub>(Mg) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(O) + E<sub>ea1</sub>(O) + E<sub>ea2</sub>(O) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(MgO) **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) = –552 – 148 – 736 – 248 + 141 – 798 + 3791 **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) = **+1450 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rearrange the Born-Haber equation to make Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Mg) the subject before substituting values. When a term moves to the other side of the equation, its sign changes.
> 
> The second ionisation energy must always be positive (endothermic), as energy is always required to remove an electron from an already positively charged ion.
> 
> Show your working clearly — if you make an arithmetic error you can still gain marks for a correct method.

parts.problem_md: Magnesium oxide is generally insoluble in water whereas calcium oxide is sparingly soluble. Explain why there is no enthalpy of solution data for calcium oxide.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> There is no enthalpy of solution data for calcium oxide because:
> 
> - Calcium oxide reacts with water to produce OH<sup>-</sup> ions in solution **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The reaction of calcium oxide with water is:
> 
> CaO (s) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> (aq)
> 
> This is a chemical reaction rather than a simple dissolution into ions, so the enthalpy of solution definition does not apply. The enthalpy of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic compound dissolves in excess water to give its constituent ions at infinite dilution.

parts.problem_md:
Calcium chloride, CaCl<sub>2</sub>, is an important industrial chemical used in refrigeration plants, for de-icing roads and for giving greater strength to concrete.

Construct an equation to show what is meant by the lattice energy of calcium chloride.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The lattice energy of calcium chloride is shown by the equation:
> 
> - Ca<sup>2+</sup> (g) + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (s) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be correct to score the mark.

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions. The equation must show 1 mole of CaCl<sub>2</sub> being formed.
> 
> Don't forget to balance the chloride ions as 2 Cl<sup>-</sup> are needed for 1 Ca<sup>2+</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
Explain how the lattice energies of the following salts compare in magnitude with that of calcium chloride.

- calcium fluoride
- calcium sulfide
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The lattice energies of calcium fluoride and calcium sulfide compared to calcium chloride:
> 
> - Both have larger lattice energies (more exothermic) than CaCl<sub>2</sub>
> **OR**
> Both lattice energies are more negative than that of CaCl<sub>2</sub> **[1 mark]**
> - F<sup>-</sup> is smaller than Cl<sup>-</sup>, so the Ca<sup>2+</sup>–F<sup>-</sup> distance is shorter and the electrostatic attraction is stronger (for CaF<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**
> - S<sup>2-</sup> has a higher charge than Cl<sup>-</sup>, so the electrostatic attraction between Ca<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2-</sup> is greater (for CaS) **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two factors affect the magnitude of lattice energy:
> 
> Charge on the ions:
> 
> - Higher charge
> - → stronger electrostatic attraction
> - → more exothermic lattice energy
> 
> Size of the ions:
> 
> - Smaller ion
> - → shorter inter-ionic distance
> - → stronger attraction
> - → more exothermic lattice energy
> 
> For CaF<sub>2</sub> vs CaCl<sub>2</sub>: same charge, but F<sup>-</sup> is smaller than Cl<sup>-</sup>, so the Ca<sup>2+</sup>–F<sup>-</sup> distance is shorter and the lattice energy is more exothermic.
> 
> For CaS vs CaCl<sub>2</sub>: S<sup>2-</sup> has a 2- charge compared to 1- for Cl<sup>-</sup>, giving stronger electrostatic attraction and a more exothermic lattice energy.

parts.problem_md:
Use the data in Table 3.1 to calculate the lattice energy of CaCl<sub>2</sub>.

Show your working.

**Table 3.1**

| **Enthalpy change** | **Value / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Standard enthalpy change of formation of CaCl<sub>2</sub> (s) | –796 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of Ca (s) | +178 |
| Electron affinity per mole of Cl atoms | –349 |
| First ionisation energy of Ca | +590 |
| Second ionisation energy of Ca | +1150 |
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) | +244 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the lattice energy of CaCl<sub>2</sub>:

- Identify the relevant values and apply correct multipliers (2 Cl atoms required, so 2 × E<sub>ea</sub>(Cl)):

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Ca) = +178; IE<sub>1</sub>(Ca) = +590; IE<sub>2</sub>(Ca) = +1150; Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Cl<sub>2</sub>) = +244; 2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(Cl) = 2 x (–349) = –698 **[1 mark]**

- Apply Hess's Law:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(CaCl<sub>2</sub>) = –796 – 178 – 590 – 1150 – 244 – (–698) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(CaCl<sub>2</sub>) = **–2260 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To calculate lattice energy, rearrange the Hess equation: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> minus all other enthalpy changes in the cycle.
> 
> Be careful with the sign of the electron affinity. The electron affinity of Cl is –349 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> (exothermic). When you subtract E<sub>ea</sub> from the rearranged Hess equation, you get: –(–349) = +349 per mole of Cl. For 2 moles of Cl, this contributes +698 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.
> 
> Lattice energy is always exothermic (negative), as forming ionic bonds releases energy. If your answer is positive, check the signs in your calculation.

parts.problem_md:
When a solution of CaCl<sub>2</sub> is added to a solution of the dicarboxylic acid, malonic acid, the salt calcium malonate is precipitated as a white solid.

The solid has the following composition by mass: Ca, 28.2%; C, 25.2%; H, 1.4%; O, 45.2%.

i) Calculate the empirical formula of calcium malonate.

[2]

ii) Suggest the structural formula of malonic acid.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
i) To find the empirical formula, divide each percentage by the relative atomic mass:

Ca: $\frac{28.2}{40.1}$ = 0.703

C: $\frac{25.2}{12.0}$ = 2.100

H: $\frac{1.4}{1.0}$ = 1.400

O: $\frac{45.2}{16.0}$ = 2.825

**[1 mark]**

- Divide all values by the smallest (0.703):

Ca : C : H : O = 1 : 2.99 : 1.99 : 4.02

Ca : C : H : O ≈ 1 : 3 : 2 : 4

- Empirical formula:

CaC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>

**[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The structural formula of malonic acid:
> 
> - CH<sub>2</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub> / HOOC–CH<sub>2</sub>–COOH **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To find an empirical formula: divide the percentage of each element by its relative atomic mass to get moles, then divide all values by the smallest to find the whole-number ratio.
> 
> For part ii): the empirical formula of the calcium salt (CaC<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub>) consists of Ca<sup>2+</sup> and the malonate ion C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub><sup>2-</sup>. Malonic acid is a dicarboxylic acid, so it contains two COOH groups, accounting for 2C and 4O. The remaining group is CH<sub>2</sub>. The malonate ion is CH<sub>2</sub>(COO)<sub>2</sub><sup>2-</sup>, so malonic acid is CH<sub>2</sub>(COOH)<sub>2</sub>.

parts.problem_md:
Table 3.1 shows the enthalpy data for the formation of sodium chloride.

**Table 3.1**

| **Symbol** | **Equation** | **Value / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> NaCl | Na (s) + ½Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → NaCl (s) | –411 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub> Cl | ½Cl<sub>2</sub> (g) → Cl (g) | 121 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub> Na | Na (s) → Na (g) | 108 |
| E<sub>ea</sub> Cl | Cl (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → Cl<sup>-</sup> (g) | –349 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie</sub> Na | Na (g) → Na<sup>+</sup> (g) | 496 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> NaCl | Na<sup>+</sup>(g) + Cl<sup>-</sup>(g) → NaCl (s) | To be calculated |

Calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride.

Show your working.
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the lattice energy of sodium chloride, a Born-Haber cycle can be constructed:

![Born-Haber cycle for the formation of sodium chloride](assets/003-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-sodium-chl.jpeg)

- Apply Hess's Law (direct route = indirect route):

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> (NaCl) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub> (Na) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub> (Cl) + E<sub>ea</sub> (Cl) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie</sub> (Na) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> (NaCl) **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> (NaCl) = –411 – 108 – 121 – (–349) – 496 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> (NaCl) = **–787 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 1 mark for directly writing the rearranged equation: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub> (Na) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub> (Cl) – E<sub>ea</sub> (Cl) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie</sub> (Na)

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating lattice energy using a Born-Haber cycle, remember that the direct route (enthalpy of formation) must equal the indirect route (sum of all other steps). This is Hess's Law.
> 
> Draw the cycle carefully and make sure you account for the sign of each enthalpy change when substituting values.

parts.problem_md: Define the term first electron affinity.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of first electron affinity:
> 
> - The enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is gained by one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge **[1 mark]**
> - Under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Learning thermodynamic definitions is important for CIE IAL Chemistry. You should also be able to represent the first electron affinity with an equation, for example O (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → O<sup>-</sup>(g).
> 
> Note that the first electron affinity can be exothermic or endothermic depending on the element. For most elements in Group 16 and 17, the first electron affinity is exothermic because energy is released when an electron is attracted to the neutral atom.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Define the term first electron affinity.

The definition of first electron affinity:
- The enthalpy change when one mole of electrons is gained by one mole of gaseous atoms to form one mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge
- Under standard conditions

A section of the Born-Haber cycle for the formation of magnesium oxide is shown in Fig. 3.1.

![Born-Haber cycle for magnesium oxide showing first and second electron affinities of oxygen](assets/004-born-haber-cycle-for-magnesium-oxide-showing-fir.png)

**Fig. 3.1**

The first electron affinity of oxygen has a negative value so the arrow points downwards. The second electron affinity of oxygen has a positive value so the arrow points upwards.

Explain why the arrows point in different directions.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The arrows point in different directions because:
> 
> - The first electron affinity of oxygen is exothermic (arrow points downwards) **[1 mark]**
> - The second electron affinity of oxygen is endothermic (arrow points upwards) **[1 mark]**
> - The repulsion between the incoming electron and the O<sup>-</sup> ion must be overcome, which requires energy input **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In a Born-Haber cycle, an arrow pointing downwards represents an exothermic process (negative enthalpy change), while an arrow pointing upwards represents an endothermic process (positive enthalpy change).
> 
> The first electron affinity: O (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → O<sup>-</sup>(g). This is exothermic because energy is released when an electron is attracted to the neutral atom.
> 
> The second electron affinity: O<sup>-</sup>(g) + e<sup>-</sup> → O<sup>2-</sup>(g). This is endothermic because the incoming electron is repelled by the existing negative charge on O<sup>-</sup>, requiring energy input to overcome this repulsion.

parts.problem_md:
One use of pure crystals of lithium fluoride is in X-ray monochromators.

The Born-Haber cycle for lithium fluoride is shown in Fig. 2.1.

![Born-Haber cycle for the formation of lithium fluoride](assets/005-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-lithium-fl.png)

**Fig. 2.1**

i) Define the term enthalpy of atomisation.

[2]

ii) Explain why the enthalpy of atomisation of fluorine is positive.

[1]

iii) Complete the Born-Haber cycle for lithium fluoride in Fig. 2.1 by adding the missing species on the lines.

[2]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The definition of enthalpy of atomisation:
> 
> - Formation of one mole of gaseous atoms from the element **[1 mark]**
> - In its standard state, under standard conditions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The enthalpy of atomisation of fluorine is positive because:
> 
> - Energy is required to break the F–F bonds in F<sub>2</sub> / the process involves only bond breaking **[1 mark]**

iii) The completed Born-Haber cycle for lithium fluoride is:

![Completed Born-Haber cycle for the formation of lithium fluoride showing species at each level](assets/006-completed-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for (atomisation of Li): Li (g) + ½F<sub>2</sub> (g), written on the correct line
> 
> 1 mark for (first ionisation of Li): Li<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> + ½F<sub>2</sub> (g), written on the correct line

> **[exam-tip]**
> When completing a Born-Haber cycle, you must include state symbols and any electrons at each level of the cycle.
> 
> A useful method for drawing Born-Haber cycles is the F.A.I.L. approach: Formation (start with elements in standard states), Atomisation, Ionisation, Lattice energy. Work clockwise from the elements.
> 
> For lithium: atomisation converts Li (s) → Li (g).
> 
> For fluorine: only ½F<sub>2</sub> is needed, so atomisation gives ½F<sub>2</sub> (g) → F (g).

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

One use of pure crystals of lithium fluoride is in X-ray monochromators.

The Born-Haber cycle for lithium fluoride is shown in Fig. 2.1.

Use the data in Table 2.1 and your completed Born-Haber cycle from part **(a)** to answer the questions below.

**Table 2.1**

| **Name of enthalpy change** | **Energy change / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Li (s) → Li (g) | +216 |
| Li (g) → Li<sup>+</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> | +520 |
| F<sub>2</sub> (g) → 2F (g) | +158 |
| F (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → F<sup>-</sup> (g) | –348 |
| Li (s) + ½F<sub>2</sub> (g) → LiF (s) | –594 |

i) Calculate the lattice energy of lithium fluoride.

Show your working.

[2]

ii) Explain and justify how the lattice energy of LiBr compares with that of LiF.

You must refer to the size of the ions in your answer.

[3]
parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the lattice energy of LiF:

- Set up the Hess equation:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(LiF) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(LiF) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Li) – IE<sub>1</sub>(Li) – ½D(F–F) – E<sub>ea</sub>(F)

- Substitute the values (note: ½ x 158 = 79 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>):

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(LiF) = –594 – 216 – 520 – 79 + 348 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(LiF) = **–1061 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The lattice energy of LiBr compared to LiF:
> 
> - LiBr has a less negative / less exothermic lattice energy than LiF **[1 mark]**
> - Br<sup>-</sup> is larger than F<sup>-</sup>
> **OR**
> Br<sup>-</sup> has more electron shells than F<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the inter-ionic distance between Li<sup>+</sup> and Br<sup>-</sup> is greater, so the electrostatic attraction between them is weaker **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When calculating lattice energy using a Born-Haber cycle, the easiest method is to rearrange the Hess equation so that lattice energy is the subject. Any enthalpy change going in the same direction as the lattice energy arrow is added; any going in the opposite direction is subtracted.
> 
> Remember to halve the F<sub>2</sub> bond dissociation energy, since only 1 mole of F atoms is needed to form LiF.
> 
> When comparing lattice energies, consider ionic charge and ionic radius. A larger ion means a greater inter-ionic distance, which reduces the electrostatic attraction between the ions and gives a less exothermic (less negative) lattice energy.

parts.problem_md:
This question is about enthalpy changes in solution.

i) Write the equation for the process showing the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride. Include state symbols in your answer.

[1]

ii) Use the data in Table 2.2 to calculate the standard enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride.

Show your working.

[2]

**Table 2.2**

| **Name of enthalpy change in solution** | **Enthalpy change (kJ m**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| Enthalpy of lattice dissociation of potassium fluoride | +829 |
| Enthalpy of hydration of potassium ions | –340 |
| Enthalpy of hydration of fluoride ions | –504 |
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride:
> 
> - KF (s) → K<sup>+</sup>(aq) + F<sup>-</sup>(aq) **[1 mark]**
> 
> Allow H<sub>2</sub>O over the arrow or an equilibrium arrow.

ii) To calculate the standard enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride:

- Apply the equation:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> KF = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt diss</sub> KF + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> K<sup>+</sup> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> F<sup>-</sup>

- Substitute the values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> KF = 829 + (–340) + (–504) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> KF = **–15 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When writing equations for enthalpy of solution, you must include state symbols and charges on the ions.
> 
> Note the sign convention: lattice dissociation is endothermic (positive value), while lattice formation is exothermic (negative value). The values are equal in magnitude but opposite in sign. The table gives dissociation (+829), so use +829 directly.
> 
> A common error is using the wrong sign for the lattice enthalpy. Always check whether the table gives lattice formation or lattice dissociation.

parts.problem_md: Explain why the value for the enthalpy of hydration, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub>, of Group 1 ions increases from lithium to caesium.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The enthalpy of hydration becomes less exothermic (increases in value) from Li<sup>+</sup> to Cs<sup>+</sup> because:
> 
> - Ionic radius increases down Group 1 (more electron shells) **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the attraction between the ion and the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen atoms in water molecules decreases, so less energy is released on hydration **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The enthalpy of hydration becomes less exothermic (less negative) going down Group 1. The approximate values are:
> 
> - Li<sup>+</sup>: –538 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - Na<sup>+</sup>: –424 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - K<sup>+</sup>: –340 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - Rb<sup>+</sup>: –315 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> - Cs<sup>+</sup>: –291 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>
> 
> A smaller ion has a higher charge density, so it attracts the δ<sup>-</sup> oxygen of water molecules more strongly, releasing more energy on hydration. A larger ion has a lower charge density, so less energy is released.

parts.problem_md:
Lattice energies are always negative showing that they represent exothermic changes.

i) Define the term lattice energy.

[2]

ii) Explain why lattice energy is an exothermic process.

[1]

**Table 5.1**

| **Enthalpy change** | **Value / kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> |
|---|---|
| Standard enthalpy change of atomisation of potassium | +89 |
| Electron affinity of O (g) | –141 |
| Electron affinity of O<sup>-</sup>(g) | +798 |
| Standard enthalpy change of formation of potassium oxide | –361 |
| First ionisation energy of potassium | +418 |
| Second ionisation energy of potassium | +3070 |
| First ionisation energy of oxygen | +1310 |
| Second ionisation energy of oxygen | +3390 |
| O=O bond energy (diatomic molecule) | +496 |
| O–O bond energy (polyatomic molecule) | +150 |
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The definition of lattice energy:
> 
> - Formation of 1 mole of an ionic lattice from its constituent gaseous ions **[1 mark]**
> - Under standard conditions **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) Lattice energy is an exothermic process because:
> 
> - Energy is released when ionic bonds form between oppositely charged gaseous ions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is one of the definitions you need to know for CIE IAL Chemistry. It is worth investing time to learn these definitions as they are straightforward marks.
> 
> Lattice energy is always a large negative value because forming ionic bonds from gaseous ions releases a large amount of energy. Oppositely charged ions attract each other strongly, and this attraction releases energy as the system moves to a lower energy state.

ii) State how Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) differs from Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> K<sub>2</sub>O (s). Indicate this by placing **one** tick in the appropriate box in Table 5.2.

**Table 5.2**

| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) is less negative than Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> K<sub>2</sub>O (s) |   |

Explain your answer.

parts.solution_md:
i) To calculate the lattice energy of K<sub>2</sub>O (s):

![Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium oxide K2O](assets/007-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-potassium-.png)

- Identify the relevant data and apply correct multipliers:

2 x Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(K) = 2 x 89 = +178 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

2 x IE<sub>1</sub>(K) = 2 x 418 = +836 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>

½ x D(O=O) = ½ x 496 = +248 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(K<sub>2</sub>O) = –361 – 2(89) – 2(418) – ½(496) – (–141 + 798) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(K<sub>2</sub>O) = **–2280 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) compared to Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> K<sub>2</sub>O (s):
> 
> - Tick only in the third box: Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> Na<sub>2</sub>O (s) is more negative than Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> K<sub>2</sub>O (s) **[1 mark]**
> - Na<sup>+</sup> has a smaller ionic radius than K<sup>+</sup> (fewer electron shells), so the distance between Na<sup>+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> is shorter, leading to stronger electrostatic attraction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When constructing the Born-Haber cycle for K<sub>2</sub>O, remember:
> 
> - There are 2 moles of K, so multiply Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(K) and IE<sub>1</sub>(K) by 2
> - There is ½ mole of O<sub>2</sub>, so multiply the O=O bond energy by ½
> - K forms K<sup>+</sup> only (not K<sup>2+</sup>), so only the first ionisation energy is needed. The second ionisation energy of potassium in the table is a distractor.
> 
> A common error is failing to apply the correct multipliers. Always check the stoichiometry of the formation equation:
> 
> 2K (s) + ½O<sub>2</sub> (g) → K<sub>2</sub>O (s).
> 
> When comparing lattice energies, consider both ionic charge and ionic radius. In this case, both Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> have a 1+ charge, so the difference is due to ionic radius. Na<sup>+</sup> is smaller than K<sup>+</sup> (fewer electron shells), so the Na<sup>+</sup>–O<sup>2-</sup> inter-ionic distance is shorter and the electrostatic attraction is stronger, giving Na<sub>2</sub>O a more exothermic (more negative) lattice energy.

parts.problem_md:
Potassium sulfide is a reagent used in analytical chemistry and pharmaceutical preparations.

Draw a fully labelled Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium sulfide from its elements.

Include state symbols for all species involved.
parts.solution_md:
The complete Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium sulfide is:

![Born-Haber cycle for the formation of potassium sulfide (K2S), showing enthalpy changes for formation, atomisation of sulfur and potassium, first and second ionisation energies of potassium, first and second electron affinities of sulfur, and lattice energy, with all species and state symbols labelled](assets/008-born-haber-cycle-for-the-formation-of-potassium-.jpeg)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for enthalpy of formation (Δ*H*<sub>f</sub>) correctly labelled with 2K (s) + S (s) as starting species and K<sub>2</sub>S (s) as product
> 
> 1 mark for atomisation of sulfur (Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(S)) and atomisation of potassium (2Δ*H*<sub>at</sub>(K)) both correctly labelled with correct species and state symbols
> 
> 1 mark for double first ionisation energy (2Δ*H*<sub>ie</sub>(K)) correctly labelled, giving 2K<sup>+</sup> (g) + S (g) + 2e<sup>-</sup>
> 
> 1 mark for first electron affinity (E<sub>ea1</sub>(S)), second electron affinity (E<sub>ea2</sub>(S)), and lattice energy (Δ*H*<sub>latt</sub>) all correctly labelled

> **[exam-tip]**
> You must be able to draw Born-Haber cycles from scratch.
> 
> Harder questions often include elements that form ions with a 2+ or 2– charge, so ensure your cycle reflects this with two ionisation energy steps and two electron affinity steps.
> 
> Arrows pointing upwards represent an endothermic process; arrows pointing downwards represent an exothermic process.

parts.problem_md:
Use the data in Table 1.1 to calculate the lattice energy of potassium sulfide, Δ*H*θ*latt*. Show your working. **Table 1.1** | **Enthalpy change** | **Enthalpy change**
**/ kJ mol**-1 | |---|---| | Formation of potassium sulfide | -381 | | 1st electron affinity of sulfur | -200 | | 2nd electron affinity of sulfur | +640 | | Atomisation of sulfur | +279 | | 1st ionisation energy of potassium | +419 | | Atomisation of potassium | +89 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the lattice energy of potassium sulfide:

- Write the Born-Haber equation relating lattice energy to the other enthalpy changes:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(S) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(K) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie</sub>(K) + E<sub>ea1</sub>(S) + E<sub>ea2</sub>(S) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = –381 – (279 + 178 + 838 – 200 + 640) **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = **–2116 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The Born-Haber equation can be simplified to Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>1</sub> + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>, where Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>1</sub> includes all the steps that convert elements from their standard state into gaseous ions (atomisation, ionisation, and electron affinities).
> 
> Rearranging gives Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub> – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>1</sub>, after which the values can be substituted in.
> 
> Remember to multiply the atomisation enthalpy and ionisation energy of potassium by 2, as two moles of potassium are needed to form one mole of K<sub>2</sub>S.
> 
> You can also use the Born-Haber cycle by starting at the lattice energy arrow and travelling around the cycle in the other direction, changing the sign of any step that points opposite to your direction of travel.

Explain the difference in values between the first and second electron affinities of sulfur.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Explanation of the difference between the first and second electron affinities of sulfur:
> 
> - (The value for) the first electron affinity is exothermic
> **AND**
> the second electron affinity is endothermic **[1 mark]**
> - (Energy is required because of) repulsion between the negative ion S<sup>-</sup> (g) and the incoming negative electron **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The first electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms gains one electron to form gaseous ions with a single negative charge.
> 
> The second electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge gains one electron to form gaseous ions with a double negative charge.
> 
> The second electron affinity is always endothermic because energy is needed to overcome electrostatic repulsion between the negative ion and the incoming electron.
> 
> Exam questions frequently ask about the second electron affinity of oxygen or sulfur, so make sure you can explain the sign difference.

parts.problem_md:
Magnesium reacts with fluorine to form magnesium fluoride.

Define the term first electron affinity.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The definition of first electron affinity:
> 
> - Enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is gained by 1 mole of gaseous atoms **[1 mark]**
> - To form 1 mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge, under standard conditions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Make sure you learn all the thermodynamic definitions for CIE IAL Chemistry. The exact wording matters for scoring marks on definition questions.

parts.problem_md:
i) Construct an equation for the second electron affinity of fluorine.

[1]

ii) Explain why the second electron affinity of fluorine is endothermic.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the second electron affinity of fluorine:
> 
> - F<sup>-</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> → F<sup>2-</sup> (g) **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols must be included.
> 
> ii) The second electron affinity of fluorine is endothermic because:
> 
> - Energy is needed to overcome the repulsion between the incoming electron and the negatively charged F<sup>-</sup> ion **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The second electron affinity is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is added to 1 mole of gaseous 1– ions to form 1 mole of gaseous 2– ions under standard conditions. The equation must start with the fluoride ion F<sup>-</sup> (g), not the neutral atom.
> 
> The first electron affinity is always exothermic (energy is released when electrons are added to neutral atoms). The second electron affinity is always endothermic because the incoming electron must be forced onto an already-negative ion, requiring energy to overcome the repulsion.

parts.problem_md:
Calculate the electron affinity of a fluorine atom, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>EA</sub>, using Table 5.1.

Show your working.

[3]

**Table 5.1**

| **Name of enthalpy change** | **Energy change (kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| Enthalpy of atomisation of magnesium | +150 |
| First ionisation energy of magnesium | +738 |
| Second ionisation energy of magnesium | +1450 |
| Enthalpy of formation of magnesium fluoride | –642 |
| Enthalpy of atomisation of fluorine | +79.5 |
| Lattice energy of magnesium fluoride | –2493 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the electron affinity of fluorine:

- Apply Hess's Law and rearrange:

2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(MgF<sub>2</sub>) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Mg) – IE<sub>1</sub>(Mg) – IE<sub>2</sub>(Mg) – 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(F) – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(MgF<sub>2</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values (note: 2 x Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(F) = 2 x 79.5 = 159 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>):

2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = –642 – 150 – 738 – 1450 – 159 – (–2493) **[1 mark]**

2 x E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = –646

- Calculate the result:

E<sub>ea</sub>(F) = $\frac{-646}{2}$ = **–323 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> To solve this type of calculation, sketch a simple Born-Haber cycle, then identify which enthalpy changes form the indirect route (all except the one being calculated). Apply Hess's Law to rearrange and solve.
> 
> Be careful to multiply the atomisation enthalpy of fluorine by 2 (since MgF<sub>2</sub> contains 2 moles of fluorine atoms), giving 2 x 79.5 = 159 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>.

parts.problem_md:
**Extract:**

Define the term first electron affinity.

The definition of first electron affinity:
- Enthalpy change when 1 mole of electrons is gained by 1 mole of gaseous atoms
- To form 1 mole of gaseous ions with a single negative charge, under standard conditions

Explain why the first electron affinity of chlorine is less exothermic than that of fluorine.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The first electron affinity of chlorine is less exothermic than that of fluorine because:
> 
> - Cl has more electron shells than F, so the outer shell electrons are further from the nucleus **[1 mark]**
> - There is greater shielding by inner electron shells in Cl than in F **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the attraction between the incoming electron and the nucleus is weaker in Cl, so less energy is released **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The three factors that affect electron affinity are the same as those for ionisation energy: nuclear charge, atomic radius, and shielding by inner electrons.
> 
> For comparisons within the same group (e.g. F vs Cl): nuclear charge increases but so does shielding and atomic radius. The increase in atomic radius and shielding outweighs the increased nuclear charge, so the electron affinity becomes less exothermic going down the group.
> 
> You should be able to explain trends in electron affinity both across a period and down Groups 16 and 17.

parts.problem_md:
The lattice energies of potassium fluoride and caesium fluoride are –830 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> and –730 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup> respectively.

Explain why the lattice energy of potassium fluoride is more exothermic than that of caesium fluoride.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The lattice energy of potassium fluoride is more exothermic than that of caesium fluoride because:
> 
> - The potassium ion is smaller than the caesium ion
> **OR**
> The potassium ion has fewer electron shells **[1 mark]**
> - The distance between K<sup>+</sup> and F<sup>-</sup> is shorter than that between Cs<sup>+</sup> and F<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore the electrostatic attraction between K<sup>+</sup> and F<sup>-</sup> is stronger **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When comparing lattice energies, consider two key factors:
> 
> - The charges on the ions (higher charge = stronger electrostatic attraction = more exothermic lattice energy)
> - The size of the ions (smaller ions = shorter inter-ionic distance = stronger attraction)
> 
> The size of ions increases down Group 1 due to the increased number of electron shells, so K<sup>+</sup> is smaller than Cs<sup>+</sup>. The shorter the inter-ionic distance, the stronger the electrostatic attraction between the ions, and the more energy is released when the lattice forms.

parts.problem_md:
Use the data in Table 2.2 to calculate the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride.

Show your working.

**Table 2.2**

| **Enthalpy change** | **Enthalpy change (kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup>**)** |
|---|---|
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> KF | –830 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> K<sup>+</sup> | –351 |
| Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> F<sup>-</sup> | –504 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride:

![Hess cycle for calculating the enthalpy of solution of potassium fluoride](assets/010-hess-cycle-for-calculating-the-enthalpy-of-solut.png)

- Apply the equation:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = ΣΔ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>hyd</sub> – Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> **[1 mark]**

- Substitute the values:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = (–351) + (–504) – (–830) **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the result:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>sol</sub> = **–25 kJ mol**<sup>**-1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Allow 1 mark for a correctly constructed Hess cycle in place of the equation.

> **[exam-tip]**
> The enthalpy change of solution is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic substance dissolves in water to give a solution of infinite dilution, for example KF (s) → KF (aq).
> 
> The enthalpy of hydration is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to give a solution of infinite dilution, for example K<sup>+</sup>(g) → K<sup>+</sup>(aq).
> 
> Make sure you include the sum of hydration enthalpies for both ions in the ionic compound. A common mistake is to use only one ion's hydration enthalpy.

parts.problem_md:
The incomplete Born-Haber cycle for sodium selenide is shown below in Fig. 3.1.

Write the equations for processes 1, 2 and 3.

![Incomplete Born-Haber cycle diagram for sodium selenide (Na2Se), with three energy levels labelled as processes 1, 2, and 3, showing species at each stage with some equations left blank for completion](assets/011-incomplete-born-haber-cycle-diagram-for-sodium-s.jpeg)

**Fig. 3.1**
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The equations for processes 1, 2 and 3 are:
> 
> - 1: 2Na (s) + Se (s) **[1 mark]**
> - 2: 2Na (g) + Se (g) **[1 mark]**
> - 3: 2Na<sup>+</sup> (g) + Se<sup>-</sup> (g) + e<sup>-</sup> **[1 mark]**
> 
> State symbols and, where applicable, ionic charges and electrons are required

> **[exam-tip]**
> When labelling species in a Born-Haber cycle, always include state symbols. For charged species, include the correct charge; for ionisation steps, show the electrons released.

parts.problem_md: If sulfur is used as opposed to selenium in the lattice, suggest the change in value of the lattice energy, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub>. Explain your answer.
parts.solution_md:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> If sulfur replaces selenium, the change in lattice energy and the reasoning are:
> 
> - Lattice energy would become more negative / more exothermic **[1 mark]**
> - The S<sup>2-</sup> ion is smaller than the Se<sup>2-</sup> ion
> **OR**
> The S<sup>2-</sup> ion has fewer electron shells than the Se<sup>2-</sup> ion **[1 mark]**
> - Therefore there is a stronger electrostatic attraction between Na<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2-</sup> ions **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Lattice energy is the enthalpy change when one mole of an ionic lattice forms from its gaseous ions. It is always exothermic (negative) because energy is released as the lattice forms.
> 
> Smaller ions have shorter interionic distances, which increases electrostatic attraction and makes the lattice energy more negative.
> 
> Both the size argument (S<sup>2-</sup> is smaller than Se<sup>2-</sup>) and the electron shell argument (S<sup>2-</sup> has fewer electron shells) are accepted as equivalent explanations.

parts.problem_md:
Use the data in Table 3.1 to calculate the lattice energy of aluminium oxide, Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>*latt*</sub>. Show your working.

**Table 3.1**

| **Enthalpy Change** | **Enthalpy Change / kJ mol**<sup>-1</sup> |
|---|---|
| Atomisation of aluminium | +326 |
| Atomisation of oxygen | +249 |
| First ionisation energy of aluminium | +578 |
| Second ionisation energy of aluminium | +1817 |
| Third ionisation energy of aluminium | +2745 |
| Electron affinity of O atom | –141 |
| Electron affinity of O<sup>-</sup> | +753 |
| Formation of aluminium oxide | –1670 |
parts.solution_md:
To calculate the lattice energy of aluminium oxide:

- Write the Born-Haber equation relating all enthalpy changes:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>f</sub>(Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(Al) + 3Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>at</sub>(O) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie1</sub>(Al) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie2</sub>(Al) + 2Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>ie3</sub>(Al) + 3E<sub>ea1</sub>(O) + 3E<sub>ea2</sub>(O<sup>-</sup>) + Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) **[1 mark]**

- Rearrange and substitute values, multiplying each term by the stoichiometric coefficient:

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = –1670 – (2 x 326) – (3 x 249) – (2 x 578) – (2 x 1817) – (2 x 2745) – (3 x –141) – (3 x 753)

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub> = –1670 – 652 – 747 – 1156 – 3634 – 5490 + 423 – 2259 **[1 mark]**

Δ*H*<sup>θ</sup><sub>latt</sub>(Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) = **–15 185 kJ mol**<sup>**–1**</sup> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The formula of aluminium oxide is Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>, so values for aluminium must be multiplied by 2 and values for oxygen by 3. The enthalpy of formation is not multiplied as it already refers to one mole of Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>.
> 
> Take care with the sign of E<sub>ea1</sub>(O): its value is –141, so 3 x (–141) = –423, which becomes +423 when moved to the other side of the equation.
> 
> Show your working clearly because  if you make an arithmetic error you can still gain marks for a correct method.
